title: A local network of implants uses your body as the wiring
gist: Georgia Tech's SWANS system networks syringe-injectable implants by sending voltage pulses from a wearable hub through body tissue, using ionic conduction instead of Bluetooth or NFC. It reaches more than 10 times the range of radio and gives more than 15 times the battery life. It has been demonstrated in pork and live rats, including limb-to-limb nerve stimulation. It carries very little data and has not yet been tested in humans.

themes.theme: Why radio fails inside the body

insights.claim: According to the Georgia Tech paper, activating Bluetooth components can cut an implant's battery life by up to 90 percent.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Power budgets limit always-on connected implants built on standard radio protocols.

insights.claim: Bluetooth and NFC signals are heavily attenuated in tissue beyond about one centimeter, and commercial Bluetooth parts need devices at least 5 mm wide, while only implants thinner than 3 mm can be injected by syringe in an outpatient clinic instead of placed surgically.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Getting below the syringe-injectable size threshold changes implant procedure economics from surgery to clinic visit.

insights.claim: SWANS puts all the decision-making in a wearable hub that emits pulses of up to 12 volts through a stainless-steel microneedle patch, while the implants stay simple: two receiving pads, a transistor switch, a battery and a sensor or actuator.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Moving complexity to the wearable lets implants be cheap, small and long-lived.

insights.claim: SWANS addresses each implant by tuning its transistor's resistor-capacitor threshold so that it responds only to a specific combination of pulse strength and duration, but the thresholds must be tuned for each body and implant placement.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Per-patient calibration adds clinical workflow cost and slows scaling.

insights.claim: Because SWANS implants are built from passive components, they draw almost no power while listening, extending battery life more than 15 times compared with Bluetooth and NFC. A complete implant measures 3 by 1.1 by 17 mm and fits through a 6-gauge needle.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A large efficiency gain that could reduce replacement procedures.

insights.claim: Ionic body-conduction signaling already has FDA-cleared precedent in the Abilify MyCite pill, but earlier systems linked only two devices, whereas SWANS networks many.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Regulatory precedent could ease the path for body-conduction communication.

insights.claim: In skin-on, bone-in pork belly, a single 10-volt SWANS pulse produced a detectable signal more than 30 cm across and up to 14 cm deep, more than 10 times the coverage of Bluetooth or NFC.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Whole-body range makes networks of implants spread across the body feasible.

insights.claim: In live rats, a forelimb strain sensor triggered a hub pulse that stimulated the sciatic nerve on the corresponding hind leg, and a temperature-sensing implant relayed a signal to a second implant only when it detected a fever above 40°C.

insights.claim: In a two-month rat study, scar tissue up to 1 mm thick grew around the implants, but raising the voltage within safe limits kept communication working, with no off-target nerve stimulation, cardiac effects, or added cell death.

insights.claim: SWANS is deliberately low-bandwidth, meant to pass key readings such as temperature rather than large amounts of data, and has not yet been tested in large animals or humans, although Abramson says preliminary large-animal studies look promising.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Clinical use is years away; it suits control signals, not data-heavy applications.
insights.quote: But SWANS is not a do-it-all in-body communication system, and it likely never will be.

insights.claim: Abramson argues that SWANS could connect today's separate neurostimulation and drug-delivery implants for combined therapies, for example timed drug delivery in epilepsy, because the protocol works with any sensor or actuator.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
